note: Archelaus reigns over Judea 'in place of his father Herod'. His mother was Malthace (Josephus).
Philip is a son of Herod the Great by Cleopatra of Jerusalem (Josephus); Luke names him as tetrarch.
Antipas is a son of Herod the Great by Malthace, full brother of Archelaus (Josephus).
On Herod's death Augustus gives Archelaus Judea, Samaria and Idumea as ethnarch.
Philip receives the north-eastern territories (Ituraea, Trachonitis and neighbouring lands) as tetrarch.
Full brothers (same mother, Malthace), and rivals for their father's throne (Josephus).
Half-brothers; both sons of Herod the Great, ruling neighbouring territories.
descendant (generations omitted): Herodias is Herod the Great's granddaughter through his son Aristobulus (Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.5.4).
Mother and daughter; the daughter consults her mother before asking for John's head. Her name, Salome, comes from Josephus.
Antipas marries Herodias, his niece and his half-brother's former wife; John the Baptist condemns the marriage.
She holds a grudge against John for condemning her marriage and uses her daughter's request to have him beheaded.
At her mother's prompting she asks for John's head on a platter.
Josephus (*Antiquities* 18.5.4) says she married Philip the tetrarch, her great-uncle; Luke 3:1 attests Philip only.

Philip the tetrarch is her uncle and later her son-in-law. Mark 6:17 calls her first husband 'Philip'; most historians think that was another son of Herod (called Herod by Josephus), not the tetrarch (debated).
Augustus adopted his stepson Tiberius in AD 4, and Tiberius succeeded him as emperor in AD 14.
Tiberius was Augustus's stepson (son of his wife Livia) and adopted son (Suetonius, *Tiberius*).
Herod ruled as a client king by Augustus's favour; the two reigns overlap at Jesus' birth (Josephus).
Augustus confirmed Archelaus as ethnarch but deposed and banished him in AD 6 after complaints from his subjects (Josephus).
Quirinius served Augustus as governor of Syria and conducted the Judean census.
Not a personal meeting: Luke sets Jesus' birth under Augustus's decree, contrasting the emperor hailed as saviour with the child announced as Saviour.
Pilate governed Judea for Tiberius; the crowd presses him by asking whether he is 'Caesar's friend'.
Antipas ruled Galilee as a client of Tiberius and named his new capital, Tiberias, after him.
Philip ruled his tetrarchy as a client of Tiberius until his death in AD 34.
Not a personal meeting: shown a denarius bearing Caesar's image (most likely Tiberius), Jesus says to give Caesar what is Caesar's and God what is God's.
Fearing Archelaus, Joseph avoids Judea and settles in Nazareth in Galilee.
Debated: only if Cleopas (Luke) is the same man as Clopas (John). The names are spelled differently in Greek, and the identification is uncertain.
Tradition, and only if Cleopas is Clopas: Hegesippus (in Eusebius, *Church History* 3.11) calls Clopas the brother of Joseph.
Debated: John 19:25 may call her the 'sister' of Jesus' mother (if three women are listed), probably meaning sister-in-law; or she may be a separate woman in a list of four.
Debated: if she is 'Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses', and if that James is James son of Alphaeus, she is his mother. Both links are uncertain.
Together at the cross; if she is 'the other Mary', also together at the tomb.
A follower who stayed by the cross.
A disciple outside the Twelve; meets the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus and recognizes him in the breaking of bread.
Debated: comparing Mark's list with Matthew's suggests Salome was 'the mother of the sons of Zebedee'.
Debated: same identification as for James; if correct, she is John's mother.
Speculative: some identify Salome with 'his mother's sister' in John 19:25, which would make her Jesus' aunt.
She followed and served Jesus in Galilee, watched the crucifixion, and came to anoint his body.
They go together to the tomb with spices.
Healed by Jesus; she travels with him, supports the mission, and is a witness of the empty tomb.
Named together among the women who supported Jesus and who reported the empty tomb.
Indirect tie: her husband Chuza was Herod's steward (household manager).
A woman healed by Jesus who travelled with him and supported the group from her own means.
Named side by side among the women who provided for Jesus and the Twelve.
Jesus answers his plea and raises his twelve-year-old daughter.
Jesus heals his blindness, and Bartimaeus follows him on the road.
Compelled by soldiers, he carries Jesus' cross behind him.
Not a personal clash: the crowd chooses Barabbas's release over Jesus'.
Pilate offers the crowd a choice between Barabbas and Jesus and releases Barabbas.
Peter cuts off Malchus's right ear at Jesus' arrest; a relative of Malchus later questions Peter (John 18:26).
Malchus comes to arrest Jesus; Jesus rebukes the violence and heals his ear.
Malchus is the servant (slave) of the high priest, who that year was Caiaphas.
After a long conversation at Jacob's well, she brings her townspeople to Jesus, and many believe.
Jesus accepts his hospitality but challenges his judgment of the woman who anointed him, through the parable of the two debtors.
He hosts Jesus at Bethany in the last week, where Jesus is anointed for burial.
Freed by Jesus, he asks to follow him and is sent to proclaim what God has done throughout the Decapolis.
The officer in charge of the execution confesses Jesus as Son of God (or innocent) at his death.
Pilate asks the centurion to confirm Jesus' death before releasing the body.
Jesus calls Levi from his tax booth, and Levi hosts a feast for him.
Identity link rather than a relationship: Levi is usually identified with the apostle Matthew, since the call stories match (debated).
Speculative: both are called 'son of Alphaeus', so some suggest they were brothers; the Gospels never say so.
Identity link rather than a relationship: Nathanael is traditionally identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in the lists of the Twelve (tradition; debated).
Philip finds Nathanael and invites him to 'come and see' Jesus.
Jesus calls him an Israelite without deceit and promises he will see greater things; he later sees the risen Jesus by the lake.
In Jesus' parable, Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side and comforted there.
Speculative link, not a relationship: two different men with the same name; some readers connect the parable's ending about one rising from the dead with the raising of Lazarus of Bethany.
Jesus looks at him with love and calls him to sell all and follow; he goes away sorrowful.
Moved with compassion for the widow, Jesus raises her only son and gives him back to her.
She persists through Jesus' testing reply, and her daughter is healed.
Jesus disperses her accusers and sends her away uncondemned, telling her to sin no more. The passage is absent from the earliest manuscripts of John.
He trusts Jesus to heal his servant with a word, and Jesus praises his faith.
